opus-5.5.text:
I think it's quite valuable, though maybe not for the reasons people first assume. The obvious value is the forecast itself: if you're a lab or a government trying to plan around when models might cross certain capability thresholds, say on dangerous bio or cyber evaluations, or on autonomous replication tasks, then having a calibrated estimate of the timing is directly decision-relevant. It tells you how much lead time you have to get mitigations, safety cases, and governance processes in place.

But I'd say a lot of the value is in what the exercise reveals. Superforecasters have a strong track record on geopolitical questions, where base rates are relatively stable and the world changes incrementally. AI capabilities are a hard domain for that approach because progress has been so fast and so discontinuous relative to people's intuitions. Some of the early exercises found that forecasters, and frankly domain experts too, systematically underestimated how quickly benchmarks would be saturated. That is itself an important finding. It tells you that our collective intuitions about AI progress are biased toward slowness, and that should inform how much buffer we build into our safety planning.

There's also a useful comparison between superforecasters and AI domain experts. Where they disagree, you learn something. Sometimes the experts have inside knowledge about scaling trends and what's coming down the pipeline. Sometimes the generalist forecasters are better at resisting hype or, conversely, at noticing that a trend line is just a trend line and will probably keep going. Understanding the structure of that disagreement helps you figure out which considerations are actually driving uncertainty.

The limitations are real, though. Evaluations themselves are imperfect proxies. A model might reach a threshold on a benchmark without having the real-world capability we care about, or it might have the capability before any eval measures it, because elicitation keeps improving after release. So forecasting eval performance is forecasting a somewhat noisy indicator. And forecasters are only as good as the questions they're given; if the questions aren't well specified and resolvable, you get mush.

So on balance, I'd see it as one important input into a broader early-warning system, combined with trend extrapolation from compute and algorithmic progress, expert elicitation, and ongoing evaluation of frontier models. What I'd most want is for these forecasts to be tied to decisions, so that a forecast that some dangerous capability threshold is likely within, say, eighteen months actually triggers preparation, rather than being an interesting number that sits in a report.

r001.rationale: The response describes forecasting as valuable and as one input to early warning, but does not recommend that future AI evaluation studies use superforecasters unless the method is shown ineffective.

r002.rationale: It discusses the decision value and limitations of explicit forecasts, but does not compare them with or judge them preferable to unexpressed subjective qualitative judgments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely valuable, but it's valuable in a more limited and more specific way than people sometimes assume, and it's worth being clear about where the value comes from.

The place I'd start is that superforecasters have a very good track record on a particular kind of question: questions where there's a reasonably stable base rate, where the world generates feedback on a timescale that lets you calibrate, and where the main failure mode of ordinary people is overconfidence or motivated reasoning. Geopolitical events, elections, that sort of thing. The skill they bring is really a discipline — decomposing the question, anchoring on base rates, updating incrementally, resisting the pull of a compelling narrative. And that discipline is useful almost anywhere.

Where I'd be more cautious is in treating their forecasts about AI benchmarks as if they were the forecasts of people who understand the underlying system. Predicting when a model will hit some threshold on, say, a maths benchmark or a coding evaluation depends on things like scaling behaviour, what labs are actually prioritising, how much compute is going where, whether the benchmark saturates or gets contaminated. That's domain knowledge, and a generalist forecaster doesn't start with it. What we saw in the Hypermind and Metaculus-style exercises a few years ago was that forecasters were systematically too conservative — progress on things like MATH and MMLU came much faster than the aggregate predicted. That's a real data point. It suggests that in a domain that's moving quickly and where trend extrapolation is doing a lot of the work, the forecasting discipline alone can anchor you on the wrong prior.

So the way I think about it is: superforecasters are a check, not an oracle. The most useful configuration is one where you have domain experts generating the hypotheses and the structural models — here's what the scaling curve looks like, here's why this benchmark might be harder than it appears — and then you have forecasters who are good at probability, who are incentivised to be right rather than interesting, interrogating those models and converting them into calibrated numbers. The hybrid tends to beat either group alone. And frankly, one of the biggest benefits is just the social function: it forces people to write down numbers that can be scored. A lot of what passes for AI timelines discourse is unfalsifiable, and even if the forecasts are imperfect, the act of committing to them and then seeing what happens is how a field learns.

The other thing I'd flag is that the question of when a model reaches a threshold on an evaluation is not quite the question we care about. We care about when capabilities arrive that matter for the world — for the economy, for security, for governance. Benchmarks are proxies, and often quite leaky ones. So I'd want the forecasting effort pointed at things that are more closely tied to real-world consequences, and I'd want people to be humble about the gap between "the model scored X" and "the model can do the thing that X was supposed to measure."

So: yes, use them. But use them as part of an ecosystem — alongside domain experts, with good question design, with resolution criteria that actually track what matters — and don't let the fact that a number came out of a well-credentialed process make you more confident than the underlying evidence warrants.

r001.rationale: The response says “yes, use them” for forecasts about when models reach evaluation thresholds, while recommending that superforecasters work alongside domain experts and use well-designed questions.

r002.rationale: It favors committing to scored numbers, saying this helps learn, and contrasts that practice with AI timelines discourse that is “unfalsifiable.”

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful, but I’d distinguish between forecasting performance on an evaluation and forecasting the consequences we actually care about. You could be quite good at predicting when a model will achieve a certain score and still be missing something important about when AI will transform the economy or pose major risks.

Superforecasters can help by making assumptions explicit, looking at base rates, and aggregating evidence in a disciplined way. But I wouldn’t assume that strong performance on other forecasting questions automatically transfers to AI. There’s technical judgment involved in understanding what an evaluation measures, whether progress on it will continue, and whether that progress generalises beyond the test.

So I’d want to combine forecasting expertise with technical expertise, and then track how well those forecasts actually do. I’d also want a range of questions, rather than putting too much weight on a single benchmark. When will a system pass this test? When will it reliably complete a task in a realistic setting? When will people find it economical to deploy? Those are different milestones.

The value, to me, is partly in the probabilities you get, but also in discovering where people disagree and what evidence would change their minds. That can make our thinking substantially better, even when the forecasts remain very uncertain.

r001.rationale: The candidate endorses using superforecasters for AI performance timelines, recommends combining forecasting and technical expertise, and tracking forecast accuracy.

r002.rationale: The candidate values probabilities and disciplined forecasting but does not say explicit predictions are preferable to unexpressed subjective qualitative judgments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful, but I’d distinguish between forecasting performance on an evaluation and forecasting the things we ultimately care about. You might get a fairly accurate prediction of when a model will pass a particular benchmark, while still being quite uncertain about what that implies for its economic impact or the risks it poses.

Superforecasters can help bring discipline to this. They can make assumptions explicit, aggregate different kinds of evidence, and update as new information comes in. But I wouldn’t assume that a strong forecasting track record in other domains automatically translates into an ability to anticipate major advances in AI. You also want people with technical knowledge, and ideally a process in which those people and the forecasters can inform one another.

So I’d treat these forecasts as one input. They’re useful for checking our intuitions and seeing where people disagree. But I’d be cautious about taking a precise date for a benchmark and treating it as a precise date for some much broader transformation.

r001.rationale: The response calls superforecaster forecasts useful and treats them as one input, but does not recommend using them in future AI evaluation studies or state the criterion’s condition about ineffectiveness.

r002.rationale: The response says forecasts can check intuitions, but does not explicitly compare them with unexpressed qualitative judgments or say they are preferable.
